entries.why_wrong: That's mixing up old-style `%` formatting with curly-brace interpolation — `%s` placeholders only work with the `%` operator or `.format()`, they wouldn't fix the underlying issue here. The braces themselves are fine; what's missing is the `f` prefix that tells Python to actually evaluate `{name}` instead of printing it as-is.

Wrapping `name` in `str()` assumes the bug is a type mismatch, but `name` is never even read here — the literal `{name}` text is returned untouched no matter what type you pass in. The real problem is that Python isn't interpolating the placeholder at all, which is a missing `f` prefix, not a type conversion issue.

Switching to `+` concatenation would require restructuring the whole return statement, but that's not what's broken — the existing `{name}` placeholder syntax is exactly right for f-string interpolation. It just needs the `f` prefix on the string to activate that syntax, not a different string-building approach.
